change.title: pr-33832-flat
change.description: Add AuthzClientCryptoProvider for authorization client cryptographic operations
change.author: Cristian Sotomayor

findings.title: Multiple real crypto providers on the classpath no longer fail; ties silently resolve by classpath order
findings.body: The old code threw when more than one CryptoProvider was found. Now the list is sorted by order() and the first one wins, and the ignored ones are logged only at debug level (lines 64-70). DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so a classpath that mixes two of them (for example default and FIPS) is no longer rejected. sorted() is stable, so the winner depends on ServiceLoader/classpath order. In a FIPS deployment that could silently pick the non-FIPS provider. The goal is for the 100-order authz provider to lose to a real one. Consider giving the three real providers distinct orders, or keeping the exception when the top two orders are equal. Also, `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a built string as the format string; use `debugf("Ignored crypto providers: %s", ...)` or `debug(...)`.

findings.title: Dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances and write the integers, then discard the results. The same values are encoded again at lines 119-120. Remove the two statements.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider
findings.body: The method returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is a JDK provider such as SUN, not Bouncy Castle. BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER (common/.../BouncyIntegration.java:34-39) is built from this value, so it becomes the JDK provider name. That is consistent with this provider using only JDK crypto, but the name is misleading. Either add a comment saying so or return null, which BouncyIntegration already handles with a fallback to the first security provider.

findings.title: Malformed DER can raise unchecked exceptions instead of IOException
findings.body: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length marker 0x80. readInteger() then calls read(-1), which does `new byte[-1]` and throws NegativeArraySizeException (line 170). A zero-length INTEGER makes `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throw NumberFormatException (line 73). The decoder's contract is `throws IOException`, and callers that handle only IOException would see a RuntimeException for bad input. Reject a negative length in readInteger/readNext and wrap the empty-integer case in an IOException.

findings.title: Test uses one default-size EC key for ES256/384/512 and only checks a round trip
findings.body: `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` uses the default curve, normally P-256, for all three tests. For ES384 and ES512 the DER signature holds 32-byte r and s values, which are then padded to 48 or 66 bytes, so the test never exercises full-length values for those algorithms. The assertion at line 56 compares rsConcat with rsConcat2, which are both produced by the code under test. An error that is symmetric in the encoder and decoder, or one specific to short or high-bit integers, would pass. Generate a key on the matching curve (secp256r1, secp384r1, secp521r1) per algorithm. Also assert the re-encoded DER against the original JDK signature, or verify the signature with Signature.verify.

contracts.equivalent_path: Other Keycloak entry points call CryptoIntegration.init once at startup. create() and create(InputStream) both delegate to create(Configuration) (lines 63, 82), so every factory path inits.
contracts.before_after: Before, an authz-client without keycloak-crypto-* on the classpath had no provider, and CryptoIntegration.getProvider() threw IllegalStateException on first ECDSA use. Now init is idempotent (null check under lock, CryptoIntegration.java:30-38) and ServiceLoader finds AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) or a real provider (order 200).
contracts.visible_effect: ES256/384/512 client-assertion JWT signing and verification in the authz client works without a separate crypto module. ECDSAAlgorithm delegates to getEcdsaCryptoProvider (core/.../ECDSAAlgorithm.java:45-50).
contracts.failure_mode: If no provider is found, init throws IllegalStateException at create() time. Every other CryptoProvider method in the authz provider throws UnsupportedOperationException, which is visible to the caller.

contracts.action: New CryptoProvider.order() abstract method and sorted provider selection
contracts.equivalent_path: The previous detectProvider threw on more than one provider (CryptoIntegration.java, old lines 63-65).
contracts.before_after: All four implementers in the repository (Default, Elytron, FIPS1402, Authz) now implement order(), so compilation is fine. Previously more than one provider was an error. Now the highest order wins, and ties between the 200-order providers are resolved by classpath order with only a debug log.
contracts.visible_effect: A misconfigured classpath with two real providers starts without an error and may use the wrong one.
contracts.failure_mode: Silent selection of the wrong provider; see the finding on CryptoIntegration.java.

summary: The change adds a minimal JDK-only CryptoProvider for the authz client, with an ASN.1 DER ECDSA converter, and an order() mechanism so real providers override it. I found no blockers. The main concern is that CryptoIntegration now silently picks one provider when several are present, and the three real providers all use order 200. The other findings are minor: dead encoder calls, a misleading getBouncyCastleProvider, unchecked exceptions on malformed DER, and a test that uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and only checks a round trip.
